e5c1682542b3.content: In the context of a decision-support table, each rule contains input and output entries. 644685d71350.title: Care Pathway candidate
644685d71350.content: A care pathway is a complex intervention for the mutual decision-making and organization of care processes for a well defined group of health service users during a well defined period (2,3). Defining characteristics of care pathways include the following used by the European Pathway Association (4,5): • an explicit statement of the objectives and key elements of care based on evidence, best practice, and health service users’ expectations and their characteristics; • the facilitation of the communication among the team members and with health service users and families; • the coordination of the care process by coordinating the roles and sequencing the activities of the multidisciplinary care team, the health service users and their relatives; • the documentation, monitoring and evaluation of variances and outcomes; • the identification of the appropriate resources. Also called: Care pathway . Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives.

83001d835c97.title: Interoperability candidate
83001d835c97.content: Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. Glossary entry (p. xi) is the primary definition; Section 4.4 body (HIMSS) and Section 4.4.2 (IEEE 1990) provide two additional definitions in the handbook. Section 4.4 body definition (p. 41), citing Healthcare Information and Management Systems Society (HIMSS). Alternative definition (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md): "Interoperability ensures that all digital systems within the healthcare ecosystem work together harmoniously. It refers to the ability of different systems, devices, applications or products to connect and communicate in a coordinated way, without effort from the end user (14)." Section 4.4.2 definition (p. 42), citing IEEE Standard Computer Dictionary (1990). Alternative definition (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md): "The ability of two or more systems or components to exchange information and to use the information that has been exchanged" .

5fb94391a1af.title: SMART Guidelines (SMART) candidate
5fb94391a1af.content: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23). Also called: SMART, Standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based and testable . Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives.

30e00d2beab4.title: Person-Centred Point of Service System (PCPOSS) (PCPOSS) candidate
30e00d2beab4.content: Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) are digital systems that facilitate the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of service or point of care. This includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable health workers to access, record and update individuals’ health information. PCPOSS also includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable screening, managing, treating, and/or communicating with, individuals. PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records (3). Also called: PCPOSS, Person-Centred Point of Service Systems (PCPOSS), Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) . Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. Section 1.1 and the Glossary note that PCPOSS encompasses 4 service/application types (community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical/health record systems, and personal health records), while Annex 1 maps PCPOSS functional requirements across 13 WHO Classification of Digital Health Interventions (DHIs): 1.1.1, 1.4.1, 2.1.1, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 2.2.4, 2.3.1, 2.3.2, 2.4.3, 2.7.1, 2.7.2, 2.8.1, and 2.9.1. Section 1.1 and Annex 1 synthesis contrasting the 4 application types with the 13 DHIs delivered by PCPOSS. Alternative definition (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-004-11-person-centred-point-of-service-systems.md): "Person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSS) encompass four primary application types (community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical/health record systems, and personal health records) and operationalize 13 WHO Digital Health Interventions (DHIs) across Annex 1." .

09b4008f459a.title: Person-Centred candidate
09b4008f459a.content: In the context of person-centred health services, person-centred refers to prioritizing the comprehensive needs of individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the centre of health systems. It involves actively engaging and empowering individuals to have a more active role in their own health and health-care decisions. It shifts the focus of health services away from specific diseases or interventions, towards holistic needs of individuals across the continuum of care and life course (21). Also called: Person-centred, Person-Centered . Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives.

Candidate definitions (4) . | Person-Centred Point of Service System (PCPOSS) (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) are digital systems that facilitate the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of service or point of care. This includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable health workers to access, record and update individuals’ health information. PCPOSS also includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable screening, managing, treating, and/or communicating with, individuals. PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records (3). Input candidate The input entry in a decision-support table is a “condition” for the rule to be met. There can be more than one input for the rule. Thus, if the input data are the same as the inputs listed in the decision- support table, then that rule is considered met – leading to the subsequent output or action. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. Candidate definitions (4) . | Output (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)In the context of requirements gathering or decision support logic, for each combination of input entries, the output is what will result in the conditions of the rule being met. This could be a single output value that would become an input in a subsequent decision table, or it could be a resulting action, activity or task in a business process. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Rule (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)In the context of a decision-support table, each rule contains input and output entries. The input entries are the condition, and the output entries are the conclusion of the rule. If each input entry (condition) is satisfied, then the rule is satisfied, and the decision result contains the output entries (conclusion) of this rule (22). Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Decision-Support Table (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)A structured way to depict a discrete decision that will need to be embedded into the PCPOSS. There can be multiple decision-support tables (9). Handbook definition, quoted. It must NOT be conflated with Registry (dpi-h-ra/registry), which is an HIE master index. | Health Service User’s Health Records (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)The record of health information, including health services, clinical observations, diagnosis and any other interactions between a health service user and the health worker or community health worker. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Electronic Health Record System (EHR) (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)A secure, online system that holds health service user health records, which include information about people’s health and clinical care. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Person-Centred Point of Service System (PCPOSS) (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) are digital systems that facilitate the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of service or point of care. This includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable health workers to access, record and update individuals’ health information. PCPOSS also includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable screening, managing, treating, and/or communicating with, individuals. PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records (3). Person-Centred candidate In the context of person-centred health services, person-centred refers to prioritizing the comprehensive needs of individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the centre of health systems. It involves actively engaging and empowering individuals to have a more active role in their own health and health-care decisions. It shifts the focus of health services away from specific diseases or interventions, towards holistic needs of individuals across the continuum of care and life course (21). Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. Candidate definitions (3) . | Person-Centred Point of Service System (PCPOSS) (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) are digital systems that facilitate the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of service or point of care. This includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable health workers to access, record and update individuals’ health information. PCPOSS also includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable screening, managing, treating, and/or communicating with, individuals. PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records (3). Rule candidate In the context of a decision-support table, each rule contains input and output entries. The input entries are the condition, and the output entries are the conclusion of the rule. If each input entry (condition) is satisfied, then the rule is satisfied, and the decision result contains the output entries (conclusion) of this rule (22). Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. Candidate definitions (4) . | Input (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)The input entry in a decision-support table is a “condition” for the rule to be met. There can be more than one input for the rule. Thus, if the input data are the same as the inputs listed in the decision- support table, then that rule is considered met – leading to the subsequent output or action. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Output (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)In the context of requirements gathering or decision support logic, for each combination of input entries, the output is what will result in the conditions of the rule being met. This could be a single output value that would become an input in a subsequent decision table, or it could be a resulting action, activity or task in a business process. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Annotation (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)In a decision table, an annotation simply provides further details and explanation to the rule, for those working on and working from the decision table. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. | Decision Support Logic (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care)A set of decision rules for standard and exceptional cases that is utilized for a decision task within a business process. This helps to reduce the complexity of the business process without losing the detail necessary for coding the rules needed for system functionality (7). Handbook definition, quoted. SMART Guidelines SMART candidate Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23). Handbook definition, quoted. df257caa1c31.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
df257caa1c31.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 4 | 182 | 0 | — | . | skos | 1 | 185 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.
